// Must-trip fixture for the unwrap ban. Every call here reaches an os.* with an
// accessor call inside an argument, and each is a distinct reason the ban
// exists.
package scanfixture

import (
	"os"
	"strings"

	"github.com/Rivil/dross/internal/pathfence"
)

// stringUnwrap: this WORKS at runtime — String() is the joined absolute form —
// which is exactly why nothing but the scan catches it. The ban is policy: the
// seam is the audited way in.
func stringUnwrap(c pathfence.Contained) ([]byte, error) {
	return os.ReadFile(c.String())
}

// relUnwrap is worse: Rel() resolves against the process working directory
// rather than the containment root, so this reads or writes the wrong file. A
// scan banning only String() would let this through.
func relUnwrap(c pathfence.Contained) ([]byte, error) {
	return os.ReadFile(c.Rel())
}

// statUnwrap and removeUnwrap cover the rest of the os verb set.
func statUnwrap(c pathfence.Contained) error {
	_, err := os.Stat(c.String())
	return err
}

func removeUnwrap(c pathfence.Contained) error {
	return os.Remove(c.Rel())
}

// builderWrite is the TYPE-BLIND case, and it is a must-trip on purpose. b is a
// strings.Builder, not a Contained, so this is a false positive in the strict
// sense — and the scan reports it anyway, because ast alone cannot tell the two
// apart and exempting the shape would silently exempt the real one too. The
// remedy is to route through the seam, or to assign before the call.
func builderWrite(p string, b *strings.Builder) error {
	return os.WriteFile(p, []byte(b.String()), 0o644)
}
